manual.title: KEEP IT BRIEF! The Tiny Pockets Library

pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
KEEP IT BRIEF!

The Tiny Pockets Library

Behind the little red door of The Dog House, a little lending library on a post with a dog-bone handle and a paw-print knob, is a library much bigger than the box. Nobody is sure how. The librarians have stopped asking.

Every book on its shelves holds exactly one hundred words. Not ninety-nine. Not one hundred and one. The Word Counter, a brass adding machine the size of a desk, makes sure of it.

Last night the Word Counter jammed. It said 99. Then 101. Then STOP. And every word fell out of every book.

You are Mystery Robot Joe, the night librarian: a tin robot with a red bow tie, reading glasses he does not need, and a tally counter where his heart would be. Step into each book, pick its hundred words up off the floor, and put thirty-two stories back together before the morning patrons arrive.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type BRIEF and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster plays the music, the page flutters and the shushing; without one, the PC speaker does its best impression of a librarian.

A cartoon plays first: the night the words fell out. Press any key for the menu, then pick Play. Leave the menu alone and Joe will give you a tour of the reading room himself.

Keys

Arrows, W A S D or the number padWalk one step (hold to keep walking)
F1Help
F2Status: it counts the words you are carrying. Words are money. Ask any author.
SpacePocket a small thing. Joe's pockets are tiny, and almost nothing in a library fits in them. Almost.
F5 / F6Save / load
EscBack to the menu

There is nothing to press to use things. Walk into a door, a book or a page, and it does what doors, books and pages do.

pages.head: The Library
pages.html:
The Library

The night is told in four chapters of two wings each: 1. Clowns and Clones (Clown Alley, the Laboratory), 2. Out of Doors (the Docks, the Backyard), 3. Home After Dark (the Living Room, After Hours) and 4. Somewhere Else, Someday (Other Dimensions, the Future Shelf). Every book's cover page says where you are, such as Chapter 2 of 4, book 3 of 8.

The reading room has a door for each of the eight wings. Chapter 1's doors are open; a later chapter's doors are barred, with a tag that names the chapter, until the chapter before it is stamped done in the Reserve Stacks. Over every door is a brass plate inked with that wing's library stamp, the one that stamps SHELVED on its returns. Nobody on staff will say who keeps re-inking them. (Gwinn. It is Gwinn. Look at her paws.)

  • Clown Alley: no running with scissors, or in slow motion
  • The Laboratory: please do not feed the ooze
  • The Docks: pirates, flutes and a paddle wheeler
  • The Backyard: street lights, clotheslines and a very well-equipped Santa
  • The Living Room: thunder (allegedly) and a broken light bulb
  • After Hours: the quiet ones, and an owl who asks whom
  • Other Dimensions: fancy catnip, Escher stairs and a superhero with his underwear on the outside
  • The Future Shelf: books from a strange year called 2026. Who is ChatGPT?

Each wing's hallway has four tall books standing on its shelves, numbered I to IV. Walk into a spine and in you go. The door marked OUT goes back to the reading room.

pages.head: Inside a Book
pages.html:
Inside a Book

Every book is a little world, acted out by whoever was in the story: clowns, professors, pirates, a ficus. Its words lie all over the floor as slips of paper torn from the page:

1a word
5a phrase
10a sentence
20a paragraph (they are short paragraphs)

There are exactly one hundred words in every book. Pick them all up.

THE END is a book with a brass lock reading 100. It will not open for ninety-nine. When you carry a hundred, walk into it: it takes them, opens, and the gold bookmark behind it puts the story back where it belongs. Then the story itself is yours to read, every word of it, and a picture of how it turns out.

THE END is the only way out of a book. In the last three wings, a brass turnstile marked 20 (a word lock) guards a corner of one book: it turns only while you carry twenty words, and the floor behind it hands them straight back. Pick up what you can reach first. Nothing in a book can take your words away, so you can always finish it. Take your time. The patrons are not due until morning.

pages.head: Shushers and Other Hazards
pages.html:
Shushers and Other Hazards

Nothing in the library can hurt a tin robot, and nothing can take his words. Plenty of things in it can fine him.

Shushers are the gray, bun-haired ghosts of librarians past. Touch one and she fines you a point off your score for every moment you stay in her way. Shhh.

Some books bring their own: the scissors in Clown Alley, static electricity in the balloon gallery, the reporters who want a quote, the exceptions thrown at those who call in the Church of the First of Zero. They all fine you the same way. A perfect night's work is 3,200 points: one for every word put back, and not one fine.

Some visitors are harmless: Doc Leo, a hobo clown with a rubber chicken on a leash; Teddy, a corgi who knows left from right; the two Sallys; a tour guide. And Gwinn, who is not allowed in the library and is in the library.

pages.head: The Reserve Stacks
pages.html:
The Reserve Stacks

The purple STAX door in the reading room leads to the Reserve Stacks: staff and robots only. A corridor runs past eight brass stamp gates, one for each wing, each topped with that wing's stamp and a little plate that reads 4.

A gate opens once its wing has four stories stamped SHELVED, and it lets you through without keeping any of them. The Word Counter checks; it does not collect.

Past each pair of gates, a stamp desk (CH1, CH2, CH3) waits in the shelves below the corridor. When both of a chapter's wings are done, walk through their gates and step onto its desk: the chapter is stamped done, a page tells you what you put back and what comes next, and the next chapter's doors in the reading room are open. It is a good moment to press F5 and save.

What is past the gates? The staff say it is exactly one hundred words long. They will not say which hundred.

pages.head: About the Stories
pages.html:
About the Stories

The thirty-two stories in this library are 100 Word Stories by Lewis Moten, reprinted word for word. He wrote every one of them for Laurence Simon's weekly 100 Word Stories challenge on the 100 Word Stories Podcast: a topic each week, exactly one hundred words each, from 2009 to 2014 and again in 2026. Laurence set the early topics; since then each week's winner, voted for by the podcast's listeners, chooses the next one, so the topics on the story cards are theirs. Every story card shows the date it went up, the challenge's week number, and the week's topic.

The challenge signs off the same way every week, and so does this manual: ...And, as always, keep it brief!

Two of the stories, The Interest We Lost and Church of the First of Zero, first went up under the name Mystery Robot Joe. He has a job now.

Only the typography has changed: a 1994 PC has no curly quotes, so they are straight, and an ellipsis is three dots. The Word Counter checked every story. It found one hundred words in each. It found ninety-nine in Steam-Powered Summer, until somebody pointed out that a hyphen makes two words into one word, or one word into two, depending on whom you ask. It is still thinking about it.

pages.head: Credits
pages.html:
Credits

Stories: Lewis Moten, written for Laurence Simon's weekly 100 Word Stories challenge on the 100 Word Stories Podcast

The weekly topics: Laurence Simon and the podcast's writers and listeners, whose weekly winners chose the next topic

Game design, art, music and every block of the library: Claude Opus 5.5

Starring: Mystery Robot Joe, the night librarian; the Word Counter, as itself; Teddy the corgi; Gwinn; Doc Leo, PhD (Comedic Science); and a great many shushers

Published by Sandbox Software. Shareware: copy it for a friend, and return it on time. Register for $10, exactly.

Parked out front: THE CHEZ, the CitiCar, plugged in at its rear passenger-side charge port. It is always charging.

Made with Game-Maker 3.0 from Recreational Software Designs.

No words were harmed in the making of this game. A few were fined.

items.title: A note from the Word Counter
items.note: Found taped to the inside of the box lid
items.address: Reading Room Desk, The Tiny Pockets Library, behind the red door of The Dog House
items.body:
Joe,

I jammed. I am not proud of it. I said 99. Then I said 101. Then I said STOP, which is not even a number. By the time I came to, every word had fallen out of every book on every shelf.

Here is what I need. Every book holds one hundred words. I will open THE END of a book for exactly that many, and not one fewer. Pick them up off the floor. All of them. The slips say how many words each is worth; I am told some of them are paragraphs. Short paragraphs.

The shushers mean well. They will still fine you, a point at a time. So will the scissors, the static, the reporters, and a twister I would rather not discuss.

When four stories are back in a wing, that wing's stamp gate in the Reserve Stacks will let you through. I check. I do not collect. Do the wings two at a time, a chapter of the night each; when a chapter's two are done, go through their gates and stamp it on its desk, and I will open the next chapter's doors. Past the gates there is one more book. Do not ask me what is in it. I only count.

THE END is the only way out of a book. Nobody can take your words in there, so you can always finish. Finish.

items.title: Library card
items.name: MYSTERY ROBOT JOE
items.back: The bearer may enter any book in the library, take as many words as it holds (exactly one hundred) and put them back where they belong. Not valid for chew toys. Gwinn, this means you.

items.title: Librarian's Hint Book
items.note: Answers hidden: use the red film
items.intro: Stuck? Find your question, then slide the red film over the answer. The Word Counter would like you to know it disapproves of hints. It disapproves of most things.

hints.q: THE END won't open. I picked up every word I could see.
hints.a: Press F2: it counts the words you carry. Every book has exactly 100, and nothing can take them, so if it says less there is a slip you missed. Look behind the furniture and along the edges.

hints.q: THE END opened, but nothing happened.
hints.a: Walk onto the open page, then onto the gold bookmark right behind it. The bookmark puts the story back.

hints.q: Why did my score go down?
hints.a: A fine. Shushers, scissors, static and the like cost a point a moment while they touch you. A perfect night is 3,200.

Top row, left to right: Clown Alley, the Laboratory, the Docks, the Backyard. Bottom row: the Living Room, After Hours, Other Dimensions, the Future Shelf. The purple STAX door on the right goes to the Reserve Stacks.

hints.q: Some doors have brass bars across them.
hints.a: Those wings belong to a later chapter. Finish the chapter you are in (both of its wings, four books each), then go to the Reserve Stacks, walk through its gates and step onto its stamp desk. The next chapter's doors open.

hints.q: Can I fix the Word Counter?
hints.a: You fix it by filling the books. It will keep flipping between 099, 101 and STOP until then. It is a very dramatic machine.
Each gate wants four stories restored in its own wing. The plate on the gate says 4. It means it.

hints.q: Where do I stamp a chapter done?
hints.a: In the Reserve Stacks, past the gates of the chapter's two wings: the desk marked CH1, CH2 or CH3 in the shelves just below the corridor. Step down onto it. Then save with F5.
Exactly one hundred words. Whose hundred is up to you.

hints.q: Some say there is a felt egg somewhere in the library.
hints.a: Libraries lose things. Good libraries keep a lost and found. The Word Counter complains that nobody can find it.

hints.q: Where is the lost and found?
hints.a: In the Reserve Stacks. Not every shelf there is as solid as it looks: look for a book pulled half out, with a red ribbon hanging from it.
Walk onto the shoebox and press Space. Finders, pocketers. F2 shows it in Joe's pocket, and a save keeps it there.

In the Reserve Stacks, walk to the bottom right corner, past the fern, and keep walking right into the shelf with the ribbon. In the Lost and Found, stand on the shoebox with the egg and press Space. Leave by the OUT door.

hints.q: Clown Alley: the scissors keep getting me.
hints.a: They run a loop inside the ring. Wait at the curb until they pass, then walk. Do not run. Do not run in slow motion either.

hints.q: The Future Shelf: how do I get the tea?
hints.a: You don't. Nobody does. That is the story.

hints.q: The Backyard: why do the street lights come on?
hints.a: They are on timers, one after another. Spooker Boy never noticed them. Now you have.

news.head: A library in a box on a post
news.html: Our lawyers asked us to keep the press release for KEEP IT BRIEF! under one hundred words, so: thirty-two stories, one hundred words each, a tin librarian who refuses to round, and shushers who fine. Register for $10. Exactly $10. The Word Counter will not make change. Keep it brief.

news.head: Since last issue: Nobody has spoiled it
news.html: Final Curtain detectives: thank you for keeping the solution off the BBS. Commissioner Hale has handed out a lot of strikes this month. The most-asked question is about Victor's safe: three dials, four symbols, no numbers. Victor never wrote anything down that he could hang on a wall instead. Go and look at his walls.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: Neighbors on the line
news.html: We aren't the only game-makers on the 412 exchange. Over on The Sofa BBS (1-412-555-SOFA), The Bard of Bizarre has been uploading song-games, each one built around a song of his. It's a different shop with a different sense of humor, and we like it a lot. Tell the SysOp we said hi. Meanwhile, THE CHEZ is parked in front of the library in this game. Of course it's charging.

news.head: In the workshop: Real depth
news.html: The office 486 has been running all night for weeks, ray tracing chrome spheres, glass cubes and one red teapot. That's our next game: Depth Perception, where every scene has a near plane and a far plane, and only the one in focus is solid. No cardboard glasses required.

news.head: Letters: "Is Macbeth the cat a suspect?"
news.html:
"Is Macbeth the cat a suspect? He was in every room I searched." - A detective, by modem

The Scoop replies: Not a suspect. Macbeth is the theater cat, and he goes wherever he likes. Most cats do.
